uses: Yarrow is the old soldiers' herb: legend says Achilles packed it on his men's wounds, and the fresh bruised herb or an ointment of it was used in folk practice to stop bleeding from small cuts. A hot yarrow tea was a traditional drink at the start of a cold or fever to bring on a sweat. It was also taken as a bitter to wake a poor appetite and settle wind, and for cramping during periods. In Sweden it was once brewed into beer.
energetics: Culpeper called yarrow moderately cold, drying and binding
caution_pregnancy: Safety during pregnancy and breastfeeding has not been established, and the EMA does not recommend yarrow then. Not enough is known; avoid it.
caution_medications: The EMA reports no known interactions, though few studies have looked. Check with a pharmacist if you take regular medicines.
caution_conditions: Do not use it if you are allergic to yarrow or to other daisy-family (Asteraceae) plants, such as ragweed, chamomile, calendula or echinacea. Use isn't established for children under 12. If a small wound shows signs of infection, get medical advice.
caution_duration: If appetite or digestive symptoms last more than 2 weeks, or period cramps or a wound more than a week, see a doctor or qualified practitioner.
caution_topical: Allergic skin reactions have been reported from yarrow, and NC State lists it as a cause of contact dermatitis; wear gloves when handling a lot of it, and stop if a rash appears.
garden_harvest_timing: Cut the whole flowering herb, stems, leaves and flowers, in summer while it is in bloom.
garden_water: Dry to average; drought tolerant and happy in poor soil
notes: A tough perennial that spreads by creeping roots and seed, so it can turn weedy in beds; deadhead to limit self-sowing. The flat flower heads draw many pollinators and dry well. NC State notes it can be a problem for cats, dogs and horses. Grieve records a love charm: tickle the inside of the nose with a leaf while saying a rhyme, and a nosebleed promised success in love. Culpeper places yarrow under Venus.
